The first few overs did not belong to Northbank in any comfortable way. Aaron Vale was there long enough to find one early boundary, but he never looked fully settled, and when Mason Clarke had him caught by Caleb Norris with the score still low, Lakeshore had the kind of opening they wanted after being sent into the field. Mason Pike then came and went without scoring, Theo Bennett drawing the mistake and Lewis Grant holding the catch, so Northbank were two down before the innings had any shape, and the whole afternoon briefly had that familiar final-day tension where one more mistake can turn a strong side into a side merely trying to survive its own start. Blake Rowan and Ethan Cross changed that. Blake’s role was less dramatic than Ethan’s, yet it was essential, because he gave the innings a long spine after the early damage and refused to let Lakeshore turn two wickets into a collapse. He did not force the tempo too early. He left enough, worked enough, and waited long enough for Ethan to move from recovery mode into command. Ethan, meanwhile, played the innings that defined the match. His hundred did not arrive as a loose counterattack or a decorative knock on top of somebody else’s platform. It came from a difficult position, and that is why it carried so much weight. At first he had to repair, then he had to rotate, then he had to punish anything fractionally short or full once the bowlers began searching for a new answer. The partnership with Blake grew to one hundred and twenty-five, and by the time Blake was finally stumped off Jamie Porter, Northbank had travelled from danger into control. That was the first major turn of the final. Lakeshore had taken the toss phase away from Northbank, then Ethan and Blake took it back over twenty-plus overs of disciplined accumulation. Ethan did not stop there. Owen Barrett joined him and gave the innings a second layer, less large than the Blake stand yet still important because it denied Lakeshore the fresh opening they needed after finally removing the set opener. Owen’s fifty-eight was a quietly strong innings, and he kept Northbank moving through the exact overs where a side can either turn a recovery into a winning total or drift back into a merely decent one. Ethan eventually fell for one hundred and three, caught by Ryan Parker off Mason Clarke, and that wicket gave Lakeshore the reward they had been chasing, but it arrived after the match had already been changed by his hand. From there Owen and Dylan Kerr drove the innings into its most productive late phase. Dylan’s twenty-five had the right tempo for that point of the innings, Owen kept finding enough gaps and boundary options, and their stand of fifty-eight made sure Northbank did not waste the work done by the top order. Lakeshore did fight back at the end. Theo Bennett removed Dylan, Mason Clarke returned to take Liam Hart, Owen Barrett and Logan Price, and the five-wicket return looked strong because it was strong. Mason was the one bowler who kept cutting into the innings whenever Northbank looked ready to open the final overs fully. Yet Northbank still squeezed out enough at the close through Jasper Reed’s unbeaten fourteen, Logan’s short hit, and Nolan Stone’s final presence to reach two hundred and ninety for eight. It was a total built in stages: early damage, huge repair, controlled middle expansion, then a slightly jagged but useful finish. Their partnership carried the reply into a workable zone, and once Caleb fell to Gavin Wells, Theo Bennett arrived with exactly the right kind of urgency. The stand between Owen and Theo was the most dangerous period for Northbank. Theo’s thirty-one came with the kind of striking that makes a revised target feel smaller: a clean hit over the rope, assertive movement into the ball, and a willingness to keep forcing the field back. Jamie Porter briefly kept the pressure alive with a quick ten, only for Gavin Wells to remove him before the burst could become a real shift. The real hinge came with Owen Mercer and Lewis Grant. That fifth-wicket stand moved Lakeshore to one hundred and sixty-six and made the game feel properly dangerous. Owen’s sixty-three was the best innings of the chase, built across three meaningful partnerships, and Lewis gave him exactly the sort of partner a chasing side needs when the asking shape begins to sharpen: quick enough to keep the score moving, controlled enough not to throw the innings away. At that moment the final was alive. Then Mason Pike changed it in a handful of deliveries. That double break did not simply remove two batters. It removed Lakeshore’s route. Nathan Cole came in and launched one clean six almost immediately, but Mason Pike removed him too. Callum Hayes tried to hold a tiny passage together and was also taken by Mason. Nolan Stone then cleaned up Isaac Ford before Adrian Walsh, who had given the tail a small flicker with eight, was caught to end the innings at one hundred and eighty-eight. The chase had moved quickly, and because the extras count was tiny, most of Lakeshore’s progress came honestly from the bat. That made the collapse feel even sharper. They had not been dragged along by wides. They had built real momentum, then lost the batters who were giving that momentum form. Northbank’s bowling card explains the defence cleanly. Jasper Reed was expensive compared with the others, but those overs were part of the wider pressure pattern that allowed Mason and Gavin to return when the chase had already become urgent. In the end, the match belonged to Northbank because they handled the two pressure points better. The first came at twenty-three for two, when Ethan Cross and Blake Rowan rebuilt the innings from danger. The second came when Lakeshore reached the one-sixties with Owen Mercer set and Lewis Grant supporting him. Northbank found the wicket then, and then another, and then another. Ethan Cross was the correct player of the match because his hundred created the platform without which the D/L defence would never have carried the same weight, but the title was secured by a fuller team pattern: Blake Rowan’s stabilizing fifty, Owen Barrett’s middle-order control, Dylan Kerr’s useful late tempo, Gavin Wells’ repeated strikes, Mason Pike’s match-breaking spell, and Nolan Stone’s clean finish.
